title: Private VPC networking deep dive - Aurelius
summary: Redwood SE walked through Private VPC networking patterns for a private deployment. Main concerns from Aurelius were PrivateLink vs NAT egress, cross-account endpoint access, DNS resolution, and performance implications for KV cache and batching. Agreed to run a short benchmark and share security docs and network runbook.
action_items: Maya: send security/compliance deck and SOC2 artefacts by 2026-11-20
Carlos: provide sample benchmark script for KV cache and batching tests by 2026-11-22
Rajesh: share current VPC CIDR, subnet map, NAT/egress pattern by 2026-11-19
Mei: list required KMS/HSM and audit log retention requirements by 2026-11-20
next_steps: Schedule 1-2 hour benchmark run with Aurelius SRE (Carlos to lead)
Share PrivateLink architecture diagram and IP requirement spreadsheet
Follow up pricing for Dedicated/private deployment after benchmark
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-18 16:00 UTC | Duration: 62 min | Attendees: Maya, Carlos, Tara - Redwood; Lina, Rajesh, Mei, Omar - Aurelius

[00:00:05] Maya (Redwood AE): hey everyone thanks for joining, we appreciate you making time for this deep dive — goal today is to walk the network patterns for Private VPC and dig into any perf implications, especially around KV cache, batching and quantization.
[00:00:22] Lina (Aurelius): thanks Maya, quick context: we're evaluating private deployment for inference of customer-facing features, latency target is 50-80ms p50 for short chats and p95 under 200ms, and we have strict egress controls.
[00:00:40] Carlos (Redwood SE): cool, that's helpful. i'll start with an overview of the networking options: PrivateLink endpoints, VPC endpoint services, and then nat-based egress. then we'll map that to runtime concerns - kv cache locality, tcp connections per model shard, and batching.
[00:01:05] Rajesh (Aurelius): quick Q — when you say PrivateLink, do you mean AWS PrivateLink endpoint services (ENI in our subnet) or the older VPC peering approach? we need cross-account access.
[00:01:20] Carlos: yes PrivateLink as in AWS PrivateLink with interface endpoints — that creates ENIs in your subnets and stays within AWS fabric; good for cross-account and avoids public IPs. peering is possible but more complex for multi-account.
[00:01:40] Mei (Aurelius): and how does DNS resolution work for the service endpoints? our DNS is split-horizon and we have custom zones.
[00:01:50] Carlos: good callout. PrivateLink uses interface endpoints with aws-managed DNS names by default; if you have split-horizon you can either use the aws provided private dns or point to the endpoint IPs. we often recommend creating a private hosted zone alias to the endpoint to keep names consistent. note: some transcription here, "Privatelink" sometimes in docs is not capitalized.
[00:02:15] Omar (Aurelius): our security team requires no egress to internet for data plane traffic. is that compatible with Redwood Private?
[00:02:25] Maya: yes, you can run the inference runtime entirely inside your VPC via PrivateLink for control plane and VPC endpoint modes for the control plane, and the data plane can be kept on-prem or in the VPC. we support two patterns: 1) PrivateLink + no NAT: all traffic flows through interface endpoints, or 2) NAT egress with strict route tables, but option 1 is preferred for zero-egress.
[00:02:50] Lina: can you quantify perf hit for PrivateLink vs native ENI-local pods?
[00:03:00] Carlos: in our internal tests PrivateLink adds about 1-3ms latency per hop compared to same-subnet local ENI. the bigger items for latency are: kernel bypass options for the GPUs, model shard placement, and KV cache locality. if the KV cache is remote you see p95 spikes.
[00:03:20] Rajesh: what's the KV cache pattern for Redwood? is it in-memory on the serving nodes, or do you use a shared redis?
[00:03:28] Carlos: Redwood's runtime keeps a local KV cache per model-shard (we call it KV cache — sometimes transcripts say K V cache or KV cash, heh), with optional prefix caching across requests. by default it's in-process memory on the inference nodes to keep L2 cache hits sub-ms. if you force a shared remote KV store you will see increased latencies and network overhead.
[00:03:50] Mei: is there support for sticky routing so that callers from our services hit the same inference nodes to warm caches?
[00:03:58] Carlos: yes we have sticky routing options at the load balancer level — session affinity/token affinity can route to the same shard. also warmup APIs and prefetching can keep KV cache hot.
[00:04:20] Lina: about batching: we have bursty traffic — how do you balance batching (cost/throughput) with latency SLOs?
[00:04:30] Carlos: we do dynamic batching with latency windows — you can cap batching delay (e.g., 5-15ms) and a max batch size. runtime will prioritize low-latency routes for requests with tighter SLOs; it also supports per-route config so you can have a low-latency lane and a high-throughput lane. note: batching helps throughput and reduces token cost but increases p50/p95 if misconfigured.
[00:04:55] Omar: and quantization — if we quantize models to int8, what's the perf and quality tradeoff?
[00:05:02] Carlos: quantization typically reduces memory footprint and improves throughput ~20-60% depending on model and kernels; latency per token can decrease because more tokens fit in GPU memory allowing larger batches. quality impact depends on model and task; we recommend running evals on your prompts. also quantized kernels have different NUMA characteristics that interact with network and ENI placement.
[00:05:28] Rajesh: routing and autoscaling — if we autoscale nodes, will KV cache cold starts cause p95 spikes?
[00:05:36] Carlos: yes, new nodes have cold KV caches. mitigations: controlled warmup, pre-provisioning, and caching tiers. Redwood supports cache migration and pre-warming via background replication of top-k prefixes, and autoscaling policies can be tuned to keep a minimum healthy pool.
[00:05:55] Lina: any recommendations for subnet sizing? we have limited IPs per AZ.
[00:06:02] Carlos: for interface endpoints PrivateLink consumes ENI IPs per AZ per endpoint, plus you need IPs for agents and sidecars. we usually recommend /22 per AZ for medium deployments, /20 if you want headroom for many endpoints. if IP scarcity is a concern we can use fewer AZs or use NAT egress model to avoid many ENIs.
[00:06:25] Mei: audit logs and KMS: does your control plane ever see plaintext data? how do we keep keys in our KMS?
[00:06:33] Maya: Redwood Private can be configured so model keys and data keys are customer-managed in your KMS/HSM. control plane metadata may flow to Redwood's control plane depending on deployment; for full isolation we provide an air-gapped option and you can opt for a customer-managed control plane. we'll share the SOC2 docs and the KMS integration guide after this call.
[00:06:55] Rajesh: practical question — what's the IP requirement spreadsheet?
[00:07:00] Maya: it's a simple CSV listing endpoint names, ports, and recommended subnets per AZ. Carlos will fill that in and we can provide an example.
[00:07:10] Carlos: switching gears to runtime perf: when requests cross Account via PrivateLink, TCP RTT adds small jitter; the important part is connection churn. keep long-lived connections from your services to the inference nodes to avoid TLS handshakes and rewarm. we prefer gRPC keepalive and pooled connections for throughput.
[00:07:35] Lina: does the runtime support mTLS/Mutual TLS?
[00:07:40] Carlos: yes, we support mTLS, and integration with your identity provider for cert rotation; for control plane we use signed tokens. for additional security we recommend configuring your ALB/NLB with client cert validation.
[00:07:58] Omar: do you push metrics into our prometheus or do we scrape your endpoints?
[00:08:04] Carlos: both options. for private deployments we typically run a metrics agent inside your VPC that pushes to your prometheus pushgateway or into your cloudwatch; we can also expose a scrape endpoint behind the endpoint for your prometheus to scrape.
[00:08:20] Lina: can we run a short benchmark — KV cache miss vs hit, batching vs no-batching, and PrivateLink vs NAT?
[00:08:28] Maya: yes that's the recommended next step. Carlos will provide scripts and a short runbook. the benchmark should be run from your app stack to replicate connection patterns.
[00:08:40] Carlos: i'll attach a shell script and a python harness that can drive requests at various qps and simulate cold/warm KV cache states. it will collect p50/p95/p99 and tail latencies.
[00:08:55] Rajesh: our SRE prefers to run in a staging VPC that mirrors prod; we'll share the staging VPC CIDR and subnets.
[00:09:02] Mei: any gotchas with DNS TTLs or resolving private endpoints in cross-account setups?
[00:09:08] Carlos: dns TTLs for private endpoints are low but if you use alias records you should be mindful of caching inside client libs. also if you use shared resolvers across accounts ensure route53 resolver rules allow the private hosted zone lookups.
[00:09:25] Lina: on cost — ENI-based PrivateLink costs vs NAT gateway egress for heavy traffic?
[00:09:34] Maya: PrivateLink has per-hour and per-GB costs for interface endpoints; NAT egress has hourly NAT gateway + per-GB egress. for high sustained throughput PrivateLink can be more predictable but depends on patterns; we'll do an estimate after the benchmark.
[00:09:52] Omar: in earlier docs I saw mention of kernel selection and attention optimizations — can you explain briefly?
[00:09:58] Carlos: sure: the runtime chooses optimized kernels based on model size and seq length. e.g., for short sequences we use fused attention kernels and reduced memory passes to lower latency; for longer contexts we swap to streaming-friendly kernels. kernel choice affects GPU memory layout which in turn affects how many requests can be batched. these are internal heuristics but we surface recommendations in the Optimize toolkit.
[00:10:25] Lina: is there any difference in behavior when deployed on-prem versus in a VPC?
[00:10:31] Carlos: on-prem introduces additional network variability and often lower bandwidth between nodes depending on your data center. we ship a node-local mode to keep KV cache hot and reduce cross-node traffic. also for on-prem we support SR-IOV and RDMA if your hardware supports it for lower latency.
[00:10:50] Mei: for audit evidence, can you provide sample logs showing request IDs, token counts, and model versions?
[00:10:58] Maya: yes, we can provide sample sanitized logs and show the fields we capture. logs can be shipped to your S3 or a SIEM via our agent.
[00:11:10] Rajesh: ok let's talk about a proposed benchmark plan — 1) baseline with no batching and empty KV cache, 2) warm KV cache, 3) batching at 10ms and 30ms windows, 4) PrivateLink vs NAT egress.
[00:11:22] Carlos: yep that's exactly what we'll provide. expect a 1-2 hour run plus data analysis. we'll include scripts to vary qps and sequence length.
[00:11:35] Lina: expected outputs?
[00:11:38] Carlos: CSV of latencies, a summary report with p50/p95/p99, token throughput, and cost estimate per 1M tokens under those configs.
[00:11:50] Maya: next steps recap: Maya send security docs; Carlos send benchmark script + IP spreadsheet; Aurelius share staging VPC details. we'll reconvene after the benchmark to review results and discuss Dedicated capacity pricing.
[00:12:05] Lina: sounds good. anything else?
[00:12:10] Omar: one small thing, do you support route tables per endpoint for fine-grained egress?
[00:12:15] Carlos: yes you can attach endpoints to specific subnets and control route tables and NACLs accordingly. also support for endpoint policies to restrict which services can be called.
[00:12:30] Mei: thanks, appreciate the level of detail — security will want that SOC2 and the KMS flow.
[00:12:35] Maya: noted, we'll push those docs after the call.

[End of transcript — remainder of the call was quick scheduling and administrative notes; timestamps above cover the technical discussion. There were occasional transcription artifacts: "KV cash" and "K V cache" show up in auto notes; some proper nouns like PrivateLink were sometimes lowercased as privatelink.]
